papers.title: Characterization of Nanoparticles in Suspension by Simultaneous iNTA and Fluorescence Detection with Single-Molecule Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Abstract Quantitative knowledge of nanoparticle properties is desirable in a large number of scientific and technological applications, but measurements with a high degree of precision usually prove to be challenging. Among a range of available methodologies, optical techniques with single-particle sensitivity are especially interesting because they can reveal intrinsic heterogeneities in a fast, noninvasive manner. Recently, we presented interferometric nanoparticle tracking analysis (iNTA) as a highly sensitive label-free technique that is capable of determining the size, concentration, and index of refraction of different subpopulations in a suspension mixture. Here, we enhance this method with biochemical specificity through multicolor fluorescence detection at the single-molecule sensitivity limit. We benchmark the performance of the combined technique, which we name iNTA-F, by distinguishing populations of fluorescent and nonfluorescent nanoparticles of different material, size, and fluorescence intensity, with an emphasis on the characterization of lipid vesicles and biological extracellular vesicles (EVs).
papers.tldr: **TLDR:** The authors introduce iNTA-F, a technique combining label-free interferometric nanoparticle tracking with single-molecule multicolor fluorescence detection to simultaneously characterize the size, concentration, refractive index, and biochemical identity of nanoparticles such as lipid vesicles and extracellular vesicles.

papers.title: In Situ Nanoscale Visualization of Stripping-Induced Failure Behavior in Aqueous Zinc Batteries
papers.abstract: Abstract Aqueous zinc batteries (AZBs) show great promise for large-scale energy storage due to their low cost, intrinsic safety, and environmental compatibility. However, their practical deployment is hindered by dendrite formation, residual zinc (Zn) accumulation, and limited cycle life. Recent studies have identified the stripping process as a critical factor governing battery longevity, yet the underlying failure mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, leveraging a fourth-generation synchrotron radiation source, we employed in situ nanoscale X-ray microscopy to visualize the morphological evolution from planar to mossy Zn during cycling at 50 mA cm–2. Combining observations of the entire cycling process with optical flow analysis of the stripping process on different substrates at 1 mA cm–2, we categorize the origins of residual Zn into four distinct pathways: (i) dendrites formed during plating; (ii) dendrites generated by crystallographically selective stripping; (iii) bulky Zn that loses electrical contact during stripping; and (iv) Zn fragments resulting from inward dissolution. Ex-situ XRD and DFT calculations further confirm the preferential dissolution of Zn(100) and Zn(101) over Zn(002). These findings highlight the critical role of the stripping process in AZB failure and demonstrate that minimizing local variations in dissolution behavior through kinetic modulation is one of the keys to achieving complete dissolution and enhancing Zn reversibility.
papers.tldr: In situ nanoscale X-ray microscopy reveals that stripping-induced residual zinc arises via four distinct pathways and preferential dissolution of Zn(100)/Zn(101) over Zn(002), identifying kinetic modulation of local dissolution as key to improving zinc reversibility in aqueous zinc batteries.

papers.title: Atomic-Scale Origin of Spatially Heterogeneous Insertion in Hollandite-Type MnO2
papers.abstract: Abstract Hollandite-type α-MnO2 is a prototypical tunnel-structured host for rechargeable batteries, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing multivalent-ion insertion remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal how guest-ion species dictate electrochemical reaction pathways through distinct occupation modes within the one-dimensional tunnels of α-MnO2. By combining electrochemical analyses, atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, and soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we directly correlate reaction kinetics with guest-ion configurations and the accompanying structural and electronic responses of the host framework. Electrochemical measurements reveal substantial diffusion-controlled contributions for both Na+ and Mg2+, whereas Ca2+ exhibits predominantly surface-controlled behavior. Atomic-resolution imaging demonstrates that, despite their comparable macroscopic kinetic contributions, Na+ and Mg2+ exhibit distinctly different microscopic insertion modes: Na+ homogeneously occupies the tunnel-center sites throughout the particles, whereas Mg2+ occupies both tunnel-center and off-center sites, with pronounced near-surface enrichment accompanied by local tunnel distortion. In contrast, the Ca2+ reaction is largely confined to the near-surface region, with no clearly detectable occupation of the internal tunnel sites. Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy further reveals spatially heterogeneous Mn reduction, with more pronounced reduction near the structurally less constrained particle surface. These results establish a direct relationship between guest-ion occupation modes, electrochemical reaction pathways, and the resulting structural evolution, providing an atomic-scale design principle for engineering tunnel-type host materials for multivalent-ion insertion.
papers.tldr: In hollandite-type α-MnO₂, the guest-ion species (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, or Ca²⁺) dictates distinct atomic-scale tunnel occupation modes and spatially heterogeneous Mn reduction, directly linking insertion configuration to electrochemical kinetics and host structural evolution.

papers.title: Light-Induced Néel Vector Reversal in 2D van der Waals Antiferromagnets
papers.abstract: Abstract Antiferromagnetic spintronics promises ultrafast device performance, yet the essential Néel vector reversal is hindered by its intrinsic immunity to external magnetic fields. Here, we propose a mechanism for deterministic Néel vector reversal in 2D van der Waals antiferromagnets enabled by ultrafast laser pulses. The core physics involves light-induced asymmetric interlayer demagnetization, which drives the antiferromagnet into a transient ferrimagnetic state with a finite net moment. This transient symmetry breaking allows the Néel vector to be controlled by an external magnetic field. We identify that the intrinsic structural and electronic asymmetries and spin–orbit-coupling mediated spin flips are essential for this process. Using first-principles calculations and real-time time-dependent density functional theory, we further demonstrate this mechanism in bilayer NiICl and YI2. Our work establishes a general strategy for the optical manipulation of 2D antiferromagnetic order.
papers.tldr: Ultrafast laser pulses can deterministically reverse the Néel vector in 2D van der Waals antiferromagnets by inducing asymmetric interlayer demagnetization that creates a transient ferrimagnetic net moment controllable by an external magnetic field, as demonstrated in bilayer NiICl and YI₂.

papers.title: Covalent-Bond Engineering Stabilizes Layered Oxide Cathodes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
papers.abstract: Abstract Developing practicable layered oxide cathodes remains a critical challenge for sodium-ion batteries. Here, by systematically varying Cu contents to tune TM–O covalency in Nay[CuxFe3/9Mn(6/9–x)]O2, we show that an optimal degree of covalency simultaneously boosts energy density and structural resilience. The optimized Na7/9[Cu2/9Fe3/9Mn4/9]O2 delivers 131.6 mAh g–1 at 0.1 C and retains 80% capacity after 500 cycles at 0.5 C. Mechanistically, the enhanced Cu–O covalency converts trivalent Cu from a conventional d8 to a heavily mixed d9L configuration, delocalizing holes across the extended TM–O network, enlarging polaron size, and “flattening the ripple” of local lattice distortions. Side-by-side comparison with an ionic Ni analogue confirms the suppressed cation migration and polarization. Crucially, the covalency-driven stabilization is not unbounded–excessive covalency rigidifies the lattice, defining a covalency threshold for optimal performance. These findings establish covalency modulation within a defined threshold as a predictive design principle for durable layered oxide cathodes.
papers.tldr: By tuning Cu–O covalency within an optimal threshold in layered Na-ion battery cathodes, researchers simultaneously improve energy density and cycling stability through enhanced hole delocalization and suppressed cation migration/polarization.

papers.title: Anisotropic Nanoscale Coherent Polariton Transport in CrSBr
papers.abstract: Abstract In a combined experimental and theoretical study, we demonstrate anisotropic polariton transport on the nanoscale in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr. While effective cavity-polariton formation emerges via the self-hybridization of ultrahigh oscillator strength excitons with a thin slab photonic mode, the absence of external mirrors facilitates spectroscopic investigation of these polaritons via cathodoluminescence (CL) on length scales inaccessible to optical excitation. This direct access allows us to precisely chart the polariton landscape with nanometric resolution, and probe polariton interference phenomena. Our finding highlights that coherent polariton transport follows the C2v symmetry of CrSBr, highly directional transport along the a-axis, while no coherent features are found along the b-axis. By extending CL spectroscopy to strongly anisotropic cavity polaritons, our work establishes this technique as a powerful tool to probe highly directional expansion and relaxation phenomena on the nanoscale, paving the way for investigating complex polaritonic landscapes in asymmetric systems.
papers.tldr: This study uses cathodoluminescence spectroscopy to demonstrate nanoscale coherent polariton transport in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr, showing highly directional transport along the a-axis and no coherent features along the b-axis due to the material’s C2v symmetry.

papers.title: Mechano-electrochemical energy harvesting and self-powered sensing via dynamic liquid metal–electrolyte interfaces
papers.abstract: Wearable devices, stretchable sensors, and soft electronics benefit from harvesting ambient energy using compliant materials, yet existing approaches often face limitations in power density, scalability, and electrode adaptability. Here, we report a liquid metal mechano-electrochemical energy harvester (LMMEEH) that converts mechanical stimuli into electricity through dynamically regulated electrode-electrolyte interfaces. Mechanical motion changes the interfacial area and drives asymmetric Faradaic reactions associated with dynamic oxide formation and dissolution, generating electrical output. The fluidity, high surface tension, and self-renewing surface chemistry of liquid metals enable rapid interfacial reformation, large reversible deformation, and stable cyclic operation. The device achieves a power density of 140.2 microwatts per square meter and scales to a 40-unit array producing 2 volts. Spatial and temporal programming of the liquid metal interfaces further enables synchronized three-phase alternating-current generation. We demonstrate wave-driven emergency lighting, self-powered pressure sensing, and real-time physiological monitoring. This work establishes dynamic liquid metal electrochemical interfaces as a scalable strategy for soft mechanical energy harvesting and self-powered electronics.
papers.tldr: A liquid metal–electrolyte mechano-electrochemical harvester converts mechanical motion into electricity through dynamically regulated interfacial area and asymmetric Faradaic reactions, enabling scalable soft energy harvesting and self-powered sensing.

papers.title: Floquet-Volkov spin polarization in spin-degenerate Antiferromagnets
authors: Jiyang Fan, Dinghui Wang, Tongshuai Zhu
papers.abstract: Periodic driving enables ultrafast control of electronic structures in solids through the formation of photon-dressed Floquet-Bloch states. However, the measured photoemission spectra are influenced not only by these states but also by their interference with Volkov-dressed outgoing photoelectrons. Here, we demonstrate that Floquet-Volkov interference can generate spin-polarized photoemission in a collinear antiferromagnetic Dirac model without spin-orbit coupling (SOC). An in-plane linearly polarized pump preserves $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry, leaving the Floquet quasienergies spin degenerate. Under near-resonant driving, photon-dressed conduction and valence bands hybridize, producing spin-dependent relative phases that are converted into unequal spin-resolved photoemission intensities through interference between pathways reaching the same Volkov-dressed final state. We analytically identify this interference mechanism and verify it using nonequilibrium Green-function calculations under periodic driving and finite pump-probe pulses. We further demonstrate that rotating the probe polarization can suppress or reverse the spin polarization without modifying the Floquet bands. Our findings establish Floquet-Volkov interference as a route to spin-selective photoemission in driven antiferromagnets without Floquet spin splitting or SOC.
papers.tldr: Floquet-Volkov interference can generate tunable spin-polarized photoemission in a spin-degenerate collinear antiferromagnetic Dirac system without spin-orbit coupling, with probe polarization allowing the spin polarization to be suppressed or reversed.

papers.title: Colloidal 2D WS2 nanosheets exhibiting high-purity single photon emission
authors: Markus Xemaire, Jakob Keck, Marco K\"ogel, Marc Brecht, Jannik C. Meyer, Alfred J. Meixner, Jannika Lauth
papers.abstract: The search for quantum emitters, delivering single photons "on demand" at cryogenic and elevated temperatures for photonic technologies is ever progressing. For example, micrometer-sized WS2 monolayers exhibit single photon emission by elaborated local defect or strain engineering. Here, we show that wet-chemically synthesised monolayered two-dimensional (2D) WS2 nano sheets (NSs) with lateral sizes of 14 (+/- 6 nm) readily emit single photons from exciton recombination without the need for substrate-induced patterning, strain/defect engineering or spectral filtering. Single particle spectroscopy of 70 individual NSs shows photoluminescence from excitons (2.02 eV), trios (1.94 eV) and defect-localized states (1.85 eV) with fast emission (t1<0.2 ns, t2=3.2 ns), allowing highly frequent excitation cycles. Pulsed at 80 MHz, colloidal WS2 NSs exhibit limited spectral diffusion, no blinking and distinct photon antibunching (g2(0)=0.07 at 5 K), thereby tackling challenges of established colloidal quantum dot systems (blinking, longer emission cycles), while retaining high single photon purity as key quality of deterministic quantum emitters.
papers.tldr: Colloidal monolayer WS₂ nanosheets (~14 nm) act as stable, fast, high-purity single-photon emitters at cryogenic temperatures without substrate patterning, strain/defect engineering, or spectral filtering.

papers.title: Reaction-Programmed Interphase Reconstruction by an Ultrathin Zinc Phosphate Nanofilm for Reversible Lithium Metal Anodes
papers.abstract: Abstract An ultrathin zinc phosphate nanofilm is reported as a reaction-programmed precursor that reconstructs during initial Li plating. Fabricated by ion-layer epitaxy at the air/water interface, the nanofilm uniformly covers Cu with a thickness of 24 nm. Upon lithiation, zinc phosphate converts into metallic Zn and a Li3PO4-rich phase. The in situ-formed Zn subsequently alloys with Li, creating lithiophilic sites that reduce the nucleation barrier and promote uniform deposition, while the phosphate-rich phase suppresses side reactions and stabilizes the interphase. This reconstruction integrates nucleation regulation and interphase protection within a single precursor layer. Consequently, modified Cu exhibits a reduced nucleation overpotential, a transition from progressive to instantaneous nucleation, and compact Li deposition. Li plating/stripping cells operate stably over 1400 h, while LiFePO4, NCM811, and sulfur full cells show improved rate capability and cycling durability.
papers.tldr: An ultrathin zinc phosphate nanofilm reconstructs in situ during lithium plating into a Zn/Li₃PO₄-rich interphase that promotes uniform Li deposition and enables stable, reversible lithium-metal anodes.

papers.title: Spin-Chirality-Driven Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in van der Waals Magnet CrSBr
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.abstract: Abstract The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) manifests with remarkable diversity in magnetic materials. Here, we establish vector spin chirality as a tunable knob for generating an unconventional time-reversal-even magnetic BPVE, comprising the chiral shift current (CSC) and chiral injection current (CIC). Using bilayer antiferromagnetic (AFM) CrSBr as a prototype, we theoretically demonstrate the emergence of CSC and CIC. Compared with conventional photovoltaic currents arising from noncentrosymmetric crystal structures or collinear magnetic orderings, CSC and CIC not only possess comparable magnitudes but also exhibit exceptional tunability. Specifically, they can be switched on and off by magnetic-field-induced spin canting, reversed in direction upon canting-direction reversal, and continuously modulated in intensity via canting-angle variation. Furthermore, we reveal an unusual optical transition channel governing both currents in CrSBr. Our work establishes an unconventional magnetic BPVE with remarkable controllability, offering opportunities for optoelectronic and magnetic-sensing applications in noncollinear magnets.
papers.tldr: The paper shows that vector spin chirality in bilayer antiferromagnetic CrSBr enables a tunable time-reversal-even bulk photovoltaic effect—comprising chiral shift and injection currents—that can be switched, reversed, and continuously modulated by magnetic-field-induced spin canting.

papers.title: Quantum Spin Wave Theory with Multi-Spin Interactions for Magnetic Materials Modeling
authors: Andrey Rybakov, Marco Marino, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Eugenio Coronado, Jaime Ferrer
papers.abstract: In the field of magnetism within condensed matter physics, magnetic systems are microscopically described by a spin Hamiltonian. Its parameterization is accessible through both ab initio calculations and fits to experimental data. Frequently, this is achieved via multi-stage calculations that either relate the parameters to observable material properties or map a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto an effective spin model. In this realm, accurate and flexible methods are essential for simulating the physical properties of the latter. The present study focuses on one such method: spin wave theory. The approach is applied to a new formulation of the spin Hamiltonian, named polynomial localized spin model (PLSM), which includes terms of arbitrary order in the spin operators. This enables the direct application of linear spin wave theory (LSWT) to the analysis of the energy landscape and spin-wave spectrum of arbitrary collinear and non-collinear phases in any realistic magnetic material. Moreover, the classical and quantum parts of the PLSM are cleanly separated. Finally, an open-source implementation of LSWT, named Magnopy, is presented. It interfaces with modern parameterization software, supports arbitrary collinear and non-collinear systems, and is designed for both scripting and standalone use.
papers.tldr: The paper develops linear spin wave theory for a polynomial localized spin model with arbitrary-order multi-spin interactions, cleanly separating classical and quantum contributions and enabling energy-landscape and spin-wave analysis for arbitrary collinear and non-collinear magnetic materials, implemented in the open-source tool Magnopy.

papers.title: Engineering Topological Phases in Two‐Dimensional Materials: A Path from Preparation to Device Applications
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Owing to their topologically protected edge or surface states, rapid electronic transport, and highly tunable physical properties, two‐dimensional topological materials (2D TMs) have garnered significant attention in condensed matter physics and materials science, and are regarded as potential candidates for quantum computing. Since the first observation of the quantum Hall effect, fundamental research on the physics of TMs has made remarkable progress. To better utilize the unique properties of TMs, the importance of material fabrication and phase engineering of topological states has become increasingly prominent. This review systematically discusses phase engineering in 2D TMs, from their growth to device applications. First, various topological phases and related 2D materials are introduced briefly. Next, the growth methods for 2D TMs are summarized. It then discusses progress and limitations in growth, driven by the requirements of characterization and application. Furthermore, the general approaches for modulating topological phases are reviewed, alongside the current applications in electronic devices. Finally, the review outlines future directions and challenges in phase engineering of 2D topological materials, aiming to promote the transition of 2D TMs from fundamental physics research to phase‐engineered material platforms.
papers.tldr: This review surveys phase engineering of two-dimensional topological materials—from growth and characterization to topological-phase modulation and electronic-device applications—and outlines challenges for transitioning them from fundamental physics to practical phase-engineered platforms.

papers.title: Dynamic Decoupling as a Strategy for Highly Selective H2O2 Electrosynthesis
papers.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical H2O2 synthesis via the 2e– oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a promising sustainable alternative to conventional industrial production. Nonetheless, its practical efficiency is fundamentally capped by the inherent coupling of catalytic kinetics, interfacial electric field, and mass transport, becoming a critical bottleneck for classical static electrolysis strategies. Here, a dynamic decoupling strategy (i.e., a temporal separation of the dominant interfacial constraint rather than a physical decoupling of involved processes) is introduced and validated on a Co-ONx-C single-atom-catalyst-based cathode, employing pulsed electrolysis to modulate the coupled processes in the time domain. This dynamic approach engineers the electrocatalytic interface through three time-separated effects of unequal weight: mass-transport replenishment during the rest interval predominantly enhances H2O2 accumulation, interfacial-field modulation across the potential of zero charge governs the selectivity improvement, and support-defect modulation enables efficient Co-site utilization. As a result, this unconventional approach promotes a 2.7-fold enhancement of H2O2 concentration over the static mode, significantly suppressing the parasitic H2 evolution reaction. Validated in a photovoltaic-driven system with over 100 day stable production, this work establishes dynamic decoupling as a smart design principle for next-generation environmental electrocatalysis.
papers.tldr: Pulsed electrolysis enables dynamic temporal decoupling of mass transport, interfacial electric field, and site utilization, boosting selective electrochemical H₂O₂ production 2.7-fold over static operation while suppressing H₂ evolution.

papers.title: Planar Focusing of Anisotropic Plasmon Polaritons in MoOCl 2 /Au
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Hyperbolic polaritons offer a promising approach for subwavelength light confinement and manipulation. While extensively explored across mid‐infrared to terahertz bands, achieving long‐distance focusing at visible frequencies remains challenging due to the trade‐off between long propagation and strong compression. In this work, we demonstrate planar focusing of anisotropic plasmon polaritons with an extended focal length in a MoOCl 2 /Au heterostructure. By integrating an Au metastructure with the natural hyperbolic material MoOCl 2 , we convert surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) into surface plasmon hyperbolic polaritons (SPHPs), enabling excitation and focusing of the low‐momentum hybrid anisotropic polariton in the heterostructure. Furthermore, by optimizing the thickness of the MoOCl 2 layer, we synergistically enhance both the propagation distance and the field compression. Using transmission‐mode scanning near‐field optical microscopy (SNOM) and quantitative methods, we demonstrate a focal length of 2.5λ and a focal spot with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of λ /5 under 633 nm excitation, accompanied by a threefold energy enhancement. This visible‐frequency long‐focus system offers significant potential for noncontact nanoscale probing, integrated photonics, and optical interconnects. The proposed heterostructure engineering approach provides a versatile design paradigm for coupling hyperbolic polaritons with multiple plasmonic excitations, paving the way for advanced photonic applications.
papers.tldr: By coupling an Au metastructure with hyperbolic MoOCl₂, the authors convert surface plasmons into anisotropic plasmon hyperbolic polaritons and demonstrate visible-frequency planar focusing at 633 nm with a 2.5λ focal length, λ/5 spot size, and threefold field enhancement.

papers.title: Unveiling the underlying spin mechanism in quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing
papers.abstract: Spin-polarized lasers hold great potential in integrated photonic devices for secure communication, optical interconnections, and advanced optical devices, offering excellent properties superior to those of conventional lasers. Quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites are promising candidates for spin-polarized lasers, because their potential structural inversion asymmetry will result in strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) facilitating spin injection and hence spin splitting of electronic bands. However, strong SOC involves a trade-off between spin injection and spin lifetimes. How to prolong spin lifetimes in the lasing regime while maintaining the optical gain make it challenging to sustain spin polarization for lasing. Here, we unveil the underlying spin mechanism and successfully realize quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing by suppressing fast spin relaxation through triplet exciton regulation using organic cations of phenylethylammonium (PEA) and 1-naphthylmethylamine (NMA). We identify the Bir-Aronov-Pikus (BAP) mechanism is the dominant spin relaxation mechanism preventing the achievement of spin-polarized lasing in quasi-2D perovskites. By modulating the reverse intersystem crossing of triplet excitons, the D’yakonov-Perel’ (DP) mechanism becomes to play a key role and results in a new-emerged prolonged spin lifetime of 35.4 ps at 77 K, which is ∼5 times that of the BAP-induced one. Consequently, spin-polarized lasing is realized below 200 K, and the threshold is 30.2% lower than that for linearly polarized excitation. This work underscores the potential of PEA-based quasi-2D perovskites in spin-polarized lasing and contributes to the rapid advancements in perovskite spintronic devices.
papers.tldr: By regulating triplet excitons with PEA/NMA organic cations to suppress the dominant BAP spin-relaxation mechanism and prolong spin lifetime, the authors achieve quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing below 200 K with a 30.2% lower threshold than linearly polarized excitation.

papers.title: Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy with entangled photons and visible-light detection
authors: Jasleen Kaur, Yu Mukai, Ryo Okamoto, Shigeki Takeuchi
papers.abstract: Time-resolved infrared (TR-IR) spectroscopy reveals molecular structural changes and charge-carrier dynamics on their intrinsic timescales, in photosynthesis, catalysis and optoelectronic materials, but requires complex sources of ultrashort infrared pulses, cryogenically cooled detectors to overcome thermal background, and intense probes that can perturb the sample. Quantum infrared spectroscopy avoids these constraints: harnessing quantum interference between the generation processes of frequency-entangled photon pairs, it reads out the infrared response of a sample by detecting only the visible partner photon, for which efficient detectors exist. To date, it has been limited to steady-state measurements. Here we demonstrate its ultrafast, time-resolved form with a picosecond visible pump pulse and a silicon detector. Each visible pulse generates photon pairs within a picosecond window; the infrared photon of a pair probes the excited sample at a set delay after excitation, and the transient response is read out from the count rate of its visible partner. We resolve picosecond carrier dynamics in a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror near 1529 nm with a picowatt-level probe, unaffected by thermal background and by sample IR photoluminescence 50 times stronger than the probe. The approach is applicable to the mid-infrared, fingerprint region, where infrared detection is hardest, and to the terahertz region.
papers.tldr: The paper demonstrates ultrafast time-resolved infrared spectroscopy using frequency-entangled photon pairs and visible-light detection of the partner photon, enabling picosecond carrier-dynamics measurements with picowatt-level probes while avoiding cryogenic infrared detectors and thermal-background limitations.

papers.title: Molecular and Nanoscale Control of Exciton Transfer in TADF-Sensitized Fluorescence
papers.abstract: Abstract TADF-sensitized fluorescence (TSF), also known as hyperfluorescence, combines efficient triplet exciton harvesting with the narrowband emission of fluorescent emitters. Yet, its performance depends on the interplay between exciton conversion, energy transfer, and molecular organization across different length scales. Herein, we review recent progress in nanoscale exciton-transfer engineering for TSF, with emphasis on molecular excited-state dynamics, sensitizer-dopant spatial control, diversified energy-transfer pathways, and interlayer sensitization. These approaches regulate exciton conversion and lifetime, balance Förster and Dexter energy transfer, and control exciton distribution within emissive layers and across interfaces. We also discuss emerging directions including kinetic matching, spatial organization, and multiscale modeling for understanding the links between molecular structure, energy-transfer dynamics, and device performance. This Mini-Review provides profound insights into transforming random blend systems into controllable nanoscale exciton-transfer networks, paving the way for efficient narrowband TSF OLEDs.
papers.tldr: This mini-review summarizes how molecular- and nanoscale control of exciton dynamics, energy-transfer pathways, and sensitizer–dopant spatial organization can turn random TADF-sensitized fluorescence blends into controllable exciton-transfer networks for efficient narrowband OLEDs.

papers.title: Finite-Temperature Electronic Bands and Phonon Renormalization Modulate Thermoelectric Transport in ZrSnPt and ZrInAu
papers.journal: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abstract: Abstract Finite-temperature thermoelectric calculations typically introduce temperature through carrier occupations and scattering rates while retaining zero-temperature electronic and vibrational states. Here, using ZrSnPt and ZrInAu as model systems, we retain first-principles-derived band- and k-resolved electronic energy shifts induced by thermal expansion and lattice vibrations and incorporate them directly into Boltzmann transport calculations. These nonuniform shifts modify band dispersion and valley alignment and lead to strongly material-, carrier-, and temperature-dependent transport responses. On the lattice side, we combine finite-temperature phonon renormalization and thermal expansion with three- and four-phonon scattering. The combined electronic and lattice effects produce relative changes in the thermoelectric figure of merit ZT ranging from −9.04% to +42.29% relative to the static reference treatment. These results highlight the importance of treating temperature-induced changes in transport-relevant electronic and vibrational states on a consistent footing for predictive thermoelectric transport calculations.
papers.tldr: Including finite-temperature band shifts from thermal expansion and lattice vibrations alongside phonon renormalization and higher-order scattering in ZrSnPt and ZrInAu substantially alters thermoelectric transport, changing ZT by −9.04% to +42.29% relative to static calculations.

papers.title: A Construction Framework for Three-Dimensional Topological Magnetic Textures
authors: Maria Azhar, Sandra C. Shaju, Karin Everschor-Sitte
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional magnetic systems offer diverse possibilities for constructing complex topological textures from simpler magnetic configurations. Here, we present different routes for constructing complex three-dimensional magnetic textures from simpler parent configurations and discuss their impact on the topology of the resulting structures. We identify four construction principles: (i) adding transverse modulations, (ii) adding structures, (iii) entangling textures (e.g. braiding, or twisting), and (iv) introducing singularities. Using the skyrmion tube as an explicit parent configuration, we show how these principles give rise to several known three-dimensional magnetic textures. We then apply the same principles to predict novel textures derived from a meron tube, which are confirmed by micromagnetic simulations to be metastable in chiral magnets. Our results establish general principles for the systematic construction and discovery of complex three-dimensional magnetic textures.
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a unified four-principle framework—transverse modulation, added structures, entanglement, and singularities—for constructing and classifying complex three-dimensional topological magnetic textures from simpler parent configurations, demonstrating it by recovering known skyrmion-tube-derived textures and predicting new metastable meron-tube-derived states in chiral magnets.

papers.title: Orthogonal Passivation of Polar Facets for Efficient InSb Quantum Dot SWIR Photodetectors
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Indium antimonide (InSb) colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) offer a heavy‐metal‐free route to short‐wave infrared (SWIR) photodetection, but their performance still lags behind lead‐ and mercury‐based CQD systems, and the surface chemistry that limits their performance is not well understood. Here, we identify two independent oxide‐derived trap pathways on the polar terminations of zincblende InSb: oxidation of the In‐terminated {111}A and Sb‐terminated {111}B facets creates chemically distinct mid‐gap states, each of which degrades carrier transport. Density functional theory calculations show that metal halides bind strongly to Sb‐terminated facets, but weakly to In‐terminated facets, while thiolates show the opposite preference; this asymmetry leaves single‐ligand passivation incomplete. Exploiting this orthogonality, we develop a facet‐specific exchange that passivates both terminations and removes their surface oxides in a single step. The resulting CQD films show a fivefold reduction in hole‐trap density and a sixfold improvement in hole mobility relative to thiol‐only controls. The photodetectors achieve 50% external quantum efficiency under 1 V reverse bias at 1390 nm, to the best of our knowledge, the highest reported for InSb CQD photodetectors in the 1300–1500 nm range, along with a 580 ns fall time and 95% photocurrent retention after 100 h of continuous operation.
papers.tldr: A facet-specific, orthogonal ligand-exchange strategy passivates both polar In- and Sb-terminated facets of InSb colloidal quantum dots and removes surface oxides in one step, reducing hole traps and boosting mobility to enable SWIR photodetectors with 50% EQE at 1390 nm and improved stability.

papers.title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model
authors: Jack Yang, Lei Ao, Sean Li
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP), particularly the foundational models for materials chemistry, such as MACE, has significantly strengthened our capabilities in studying the complex dynamics of materials through statistical sampling. Here, by performing molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE model, that are further combined with essential dynamics analysis, a tool that is commonly applied in (bio)molecular simulations, we examine the temperature-dependent ion dynamics in a prototypical inorganic solid superionic conductor, namely argyrodite Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl. Our analyses show clear localised phonon-like dynamics for Li$^+$ ions below 500 K with trajectories lying in a low-dimensional manifold that is highly nonlinear, which is opposite to the case in the high-temperature ($\sim$800 K) end. Between 500-700 K, the system exhibit strong competition in the dynamics between the Li$^+$ and framework ions, that are reflected in both the eigenspectrum and the projected low-dimensional embeddings characterising these dynamics not showing a simple monotonic dependency upon rising temperatures, and is further supported by investigations employing Langevin dynamics that systematically examine how damping the framework motions affects the dynamics of the Li$^+$ ions, thanks to the computational efficiency provided by MLIP. This work thus contributes towards the broader theoretical and data-driven framework for studying the lattice dynamics of solids.
papers.tldr: Using a fine-tuned MACE machine-learning interatomic potential combined with molecular dynamics and essential-dynamics analysis, this study reveals temperature-dependent Li⁺ dynamics in Li₆PS₅Cl—localized phonon-like motion on a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold at low temperature, large-amplitude superionic diffusion at high temperature, and competitive Li⁺/framework dynamics with nonmonotonic behavior in the 500–700 K transition regime.

papers.title: Hyperbolic Nanocavities for Single-Molecule Vibrational Strong Coupling
authors: Stavros Athanasiou, Olivier J. F. Martin, Francisco J. Garc\'ia-Vidal, Johannes Feist
papers.abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in low-loss anisotropic materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide extreme sub-diffractional field confinement in the mid-infrared, making them attractive for enhancing the interaction of light with molecular vibrations. Collective vibrational strong coupling between molecular ensembles and HPhPs has already been demonstrated in extended slabs. Reaching this regime with a single molecule, however, remains a major challenge, and would provide a platform for investigating how vacuum electromagnetic fields influence molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. Here, we show theoretically that single-molecule vibrational strong coupling can be reached in hBN nanocavities that laterally confine HPhPs within a finite volume. Combining full-wave electromagnetic simulations with the few-mode quantization approach, we find that these nanocavities support a rich set of asymmetric resonances that strongly enhance the local spectral density, with frequencies that follow from simple HPhP ray trajectories and can be tuned through the cavity aspect ratio. We identify resonances with quality factors of about $600$ and effective mode volumes of $|V_{\mathrm{eff}}| \sim 10^{-7}\lambda^{3}$, sufficient for single-molecule strong coupling with vibrational transitions with dipole moments on the order of $1\,\mathrm{D}$. These results establish hyperbolic nanocavities as a promising platform for single-molecule vibrational strong coupling and open new routes toward the local control of vibrational dynamics and molecular energy flow.
papers.tldr: The paper theoretically shows that hexagonal boron nitride hyperbolic nanocavities laterally confine hyperbolic phonon polaritons into high-quality, deeply subwavelength modes, enabling vibrational strong coupling with a single molecule.

papers.title: Toward Nanoscale Chemical Clarity: THz-Pulsed Atom Probe Tomography for Hydrated Biological Materials
papers.abstract: Abstract Chemically resolved analysis of fragile biomolecular systems remains challenging because nanoscale spatial information must be obtained without compromising the mass-spectral clarity. Ferritin serves as an effective nanoscale model system featuring an organic protein shell surrounding an Fe-rich mineral core. Here, ferritin-containing hydrated specimens were prepared using graphene encapsulation and analyzed by THz-pulsed atom probe tomography. Compared with conventional laser-pulsing conditions, THz excitation improved peak definition and reduced spectral background, enabling detection of Fe-containing ions and isolation of an Fe-rich cluster consistent with the ferritin core. Although molecular overlaps and low ion counts still limit unambiguous peak assignment, isotopic, spatial, and signal-quality analyses support the identification of an Fe-rich region within an organic environment with further improvements expected at increased electric field strength. These results demonstrate that terahertz-pulsed atom probe tomography substantially improves the chemical readability of hydrated biological materials, opening new perspectives for their nanoscale studies.
papers.tldr: THz-pulsed atom probe tomography of graphene-encapsulated hydrated ferritin improves spectral clarity and enables nanoscale detection of an Fe-rich core within an organic protein environment.

papers.title: Spin swapping mediated by spin-orbital textures in centrosymmetric multiorbital materials
authors: Chengyuan Cai, Hanchen Wang, Rui-Chun Xiao, Tao Yu
papers.abstract: Spin swapping converts a primary spin current into a secondary one by interchanging its flow and spin-polarization directions, attributed to spin-orbit scattering or spin-band splitting. Here we uncover a fundamentally distinct route to spin swapping arising from the orbital degree of freedom in the spin pumping to centrosymmetric multiorbital materials \textit{without spin-band splitting}. When the dynamical proximity ferromagnet injects a longitudinal spin current flowing normal to the interface, spin-orbit-entangled orbital textures redirect the injected spins into longitudinal and transverse orbital currents. Their subsequent conversion back to the spin sector generates transverse spin currents with propagation and polarization directions swapped relative to the primary spin current. The swapping efficiency achieves $50\%$ for Ge and Si. Governed by a fourth-rank tensor constrained by crystalline symmetry and without requiring spin-orbit scattering or inversion symmetry breaking, our finding reveals spin-orbital textures as hidden intermediate channels of spin swapping with unexplored material choices and functionalities.
papers.tldr: This paper reveals a new spin-swapping mechanism in centrosymmetric multiorbital materials where spin-orbit-entangled orbital textures mediate conversion between spin and orbital currents—without spin-band splitting or spin-orbit scattering—achieving up to 50% swapping efficiency in Ge and Si.

papers.title: Electronic Structure Perspective on Cation and Anion Redox in Li2FeS2
papers.abstract: Abstract Multielectron redox in Li2FeS2 involves both cation and anion contributions. While prior studies have investigated this process experimentally, questions remain about the Fe-to-S redox transition, persulfide formation, and incomplete delithiation. Here, we revisit the electrochemistry of Li2FeS2 using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Initial Fe oxidation is shown to proceed via increased Fe−S covalency driven by ligand-to-metal rehybridization. This accounts for only ∼60% of the Fe capacity, after which phase separation into Li1.5FeS2 and Li0.5FeS2 induces a shift to S oxidation. We identify nonbonding S 3p orbitals as redox-active centers. To track their evolution during delithiation, we isolate the localized nonbonding states by subtracting the bonding and antibonding contributions from the total electronic densities of states. These orbitals undergo S-to-Fe rehybridization, progressive oxidation, and eventual reorganization into persulfide bonds. At high states of charge, Li vacancies enable FeS4 tilting and facilitate S−S bond formation. Further delithiation beyond Li0.5FeS2 would require unstable S hole formation or conversion to pyrite FeS2, explaining why it is challenging to fully delithiate this material. These findings offer insights into the interplay of cation and anion redox, guiding the design of high-capacity sulfide cathodes.
papers.tldr: DFT calculations show that Li₂FeS₂ delithiation shifts from Fe oxidation via increased Fe–S covalency to nonbonding S 3p oxidation and persulfide formation after phase separation, while further delithiation is hindered by unstable S-hole formation or conversion to pyrite FeS₂.

papers.title: Spatial structure of surface plasmon resonance under narrow-beam illumination and its implications for sensing
authors: Tristan Miralles, R\'emi Poll\`es, Pauline Bennet, Denis Langevin, Martine Mihailovic, Emmanuel Centeno, Jack Mock, David R. Smith, Antoine Moreau
papers.abstract: The reflection of light on a surface plasmon resonance structure can be understood as the interference between the direct Fresnel reflection and the light radiated back by the plasmon as it propagates along the metal film. When the beam waist is only an order of magnitude larger than the surface plasmon propagation length, these two contributions separate spatially, and their destructive interference localizes into a dark fringe within the reflected beam. We develop an analytical model of this effect, design a realistic setup based on off-the-shelf components to observe it, and simulate the complete experiment, from illumination to detection, with an open-source framework. In the regime where the interference is maximized, the spatial structure of the reflected beam becomes extremely sensitive to the outer medium. This allows us to define an observable more than an order of magnitude more sensitive than amplitude-based measurements, and we expect a comparable improvement in resolution.
papers.tldr: Under narrow-beam illumination, the two interfering contributions to surface plasmon resonance reflection—direct Fresnel reflection and plasmon re-radiation—spatially separate into a localized dark fringe called the Interferometric Reflectivity Dip, whose intensity is extremely sensitive to the outer medium and enables a sensing observable over an order of magnitude more sensitive than conventional amplitude-based SPR measurements.

papers.title: Longitudinal and Transverse Thermoelectric Properties in Topological Quantum Materials
authors: Jyoti Duhan, Anil Kumar B. M., Satya N. Guin, Koushik Pal
papers.abstract: Thermoelectric materials can be topologically trivial or non-trivial, enabling reversible interconversion of heat and electricity using a solid-state technology. Incidentally, few of the first experimentally discovered 3D topological materials, namely, Bi, Sb, Sn and Pb-based chalcogenides, were long known as good thermoelectric materials. In these compounds, the heavy atoms that give rise to strong spin-orbit coupling often become essential for band inversion and non-trivial band topology. They lead to low lattice thermal conductivity, linearly dispersing Dirac-like bands induce high electrical mobility, and a band-inverted electronic structure with multiple band extrema gives rise to high Seebeck coefficients. In materials, where the applied temperature gradient induces electrical voltage (Seebeck effect) in the same direction, they are termed as longitudinal thermoelectrics. On the other hand, when the generated electrical voltage and applied thermal current remain orthogonal to each other, the materials are termed as transverse thermoelectrics. The transverse response can be driven by an additional external magnetic field (ordinary Nernst effect), intrinsic remanent magnetisation, or non-zero Berry curvature of a material, which arises from their non-trivial topology (anomalous Nernst effect). We discuss another class of quantum materials, known as goniopolar materials, that exhibit axis-dependent conduction polarity and hence transverse thermoelectric effects, which are based on mechanisms of longitudinal thermoelectric properties. In this review, we cover both types of thermoelectricity, focusing on materials that possess non-trivial topological order. We make connections between their structures, topology and transport properties and suggest tunability of thermoelectric properties going beyond conventional mechanisms such as electron-phonon interactions.
papers.tldr: This review examines longitudinal and transverse thermoelectric properties in topological quantum materials, connecting band topology, spin-orbit coupling, Berry curvature, and goniopolar transport to Seebeck/Nernst effects and potential pathways for tuning thermoelectric performance beyond conventional mechanisms.

papers.title: Unlocking the Potential of Magnesium‐Based Hydrogen Storage Composites via Advanced Thermodynamic and Kinetic Tuning Strategies
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The development of efficient and safe solid‐state hydrogen storage technologies is pivotal for the transition toward sustainable clean energy. Magnesium is a promising hydrogen carrier due to its high gravimetric (7.6 wt.% for MgH 2 ) and volumetric storage capacity (110 kg m −3 ), abundance, and excellent reversibility. However, the practical application of Mg‐based materials is hindered by their high thermodynamic stability (ΔH = −74.7 kJ mol −1 H 2 ) and sluggish sorption kinetics. Here, we overview the latest advances in Mg‐based composites for high hydrogen storage performance. We discuss key material modification strategies, including catalysis, nanostructuring, alloying, and external field assistance to tune the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of Mg‐based materials. We stress the emerging role of machine learning in accelerating material design, performance prediction, and optimization. We also critically assess the techno‐economic viability of Mg‐based hydrogen storage within integrated hydrogen value chains. This assessment considers how storage connects with hydrogen production, transport, and end‐use applications. Finally, we outline challenges and future research directions, aiming to guide the rational design of next‐generation Mg‐based hydrogen storage materials and systems toward commercial applications.
papers.tldr: This review summarizes recent strategies—catalysis, nanostructuring, alloying, external-field assistance, and machine learning—for tuning the thermodynamics and kinetics of Mg-based hydrogen storage composites, while assessing their techno-economic viability and outlining challenges for commercialization.
